entries.name: Broken Object Level Authorization
entries.description: APIs tend to expose endpoints that handle object identifiers, creating a wide attack surface of Object Level Access Control issues. Object level authorization checks should be considered in every function that accesses a data source using an ID from the user.

entries.name: Broken Authentication
entries.description: Authentication mechanisms are often implemented incorrectly, allowing attackers to compromise authentication tokens or to exploit implementation flaws to assume other users' identities temporarily or permanently.

entries.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
entries.description: Combines Excessive Data Exposure and Mass Assignment, focusing on the root cause: the lack of or improper authorization validation at the object property level, leading to information exposure or manipulation by unauthorized parties.

entries.name: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
entries.description: Satisfying API requests requires resources such as network bandwidth, CPU, memory, and storage. Lack of limits on pagination size, batching, upload size, or request rates enables denial of service or operational cost inflation.

entries.name: Broken Function Level Authorization
entries.description: Complex access control policies with different hierarchies, groups, and roles, and an unclear separation between administrative and regular functions, tend to lead to authorization flaws allowing regular users to invoke privileged endpoints.

entries.name: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
entries.description: APIs vulnerable to this risk expose a business flow such as buying a ticket, posting a comment, or redeeming a coupon without compensating for how excessive automated use could harm the business.

entries.name: Server Side Request Forgery
entries.description: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) flaws can occur when an API is fetching a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URI, allowing an attacker to coerce the application to send crafted requests to unexpected destinations.

entries.name: Security Misconfiguration
entries.description: APIs and the systems supporting them typically contain complex configurations. Missing hardening, permissive CORS, verbose error messages, unpatched stacks, or unnecessary HTTP methods expose sensitive details or direct access.

entries.name: Improper Inventory Management
entries.description: APIs tend to expose more endpoints than traditional web applications, making proper and updated documentation highly important. Deprecated versions, exposed staging hosts, and undocumented endpoints widen the attack surface.

entries.name: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
entries.description: Developers tend to trust data received from third-party APIs more than user input, adopting weaker security standards. Attackers may compromise or spoof integrated third-party services to inject malicious data or redirects.
